title: Composition, Skipping, Anonymous Markers, Bitmaps & Text Surfaces
description: One keyframe composing any axes, a scroller that skips the unseen, nameless markers, runtime cursors, your own text surface.

drops.title: Composable Motion
drops.description: One @keyframes rule and seven typed custom properties — switch an axis on and it joins the entrance, off and it contributes nothing.
drops.concept: AnimXYZ's idea is that an entrance animation should be additive: instead of a keyframe per combination, every axis lives in its own custom property whose default is the resting value, and a single keyframe interpolates all of them at once. Reimplemented here with registered @property values so translate, rotate, scale, skew, opacity and blur each animate as their real type, with the stagger driven by a per-element --i. Toggle any subset of the seven axes and the same rule re-reads them.
drops.source: ingram-projects/animxyz — the composable CSS animation library

interaction.mouse: Toggle axis chips, drag duration, stagger and overshoot; press Replay to restart all 12 tiles.
interaction.click: Each chip adds or removes one variable from the composition.
interaction.touch: The panel stacks above the deck and every control is tappable; groups replay on scroll.

drops.title: Paint Only What Shows
drops.description: 3,200 elements across three scrollers, about sixty of them actually laid out — and the browser reports every change of mind.
drops.concept: content-visibility: auto lets an element skip layout, style and paint until it nears the viewport, while contain-intrinsic-size keeps the scrollbar honest about content that has never been measured. The counters here are driven by contentvisibilityautostatechange, the event that tells you when to start or stop your own work in step with the browser. A fourth panel shows where it does not work: identical CSS on real table rows skips nothing, because containment cannot apply to internal table elements.
drops.source: web.dev — content-visibility: the new CSS property that boosts rendering performance

interaction.mouse: Scroll each of the three panels and watch the rendered count track the viewport.
interaction.click: Toggle skipping off to feel the difference, or turn the rendered outlines off.
interaction.touch: All three scrollers have contained overscroll so flicking one never scrolls the page.

drops.title: Markers Without a Name
drops.description: symbols() builds a counter style inline, and the five counting systems each read one symbol list differently.
drops.concept: Landing in Chrome 155, symbols() lets a counter style be written where it is used — in list-style-type, in the shorthand, inside counter() — instead of being declared as a named @counter-style first. The five systems read the same symbols in completely different ways: cyclic repeats, numeric treats them as digits, alphabetic counts like spreadsheet columns, fixed runs out and hands over to numbers, symbolic doubles them up per cycle. A live editor rebuilds the style as you type, and where symbols() is missing the page mirrors it with generated @counter-style rules — which is exactly the boilerplate the inline form removes.
drops.source: CSS-Tricks Almanac — symbols(), shipping in Chrome 155

interaction.mouse: Type symbols into the panel and pick a system; every marker in the last list re-reads them.
interaction.click: The five system chips switch how the same symbol list is counted.
interaction.touch: The panel moves inline above the lists on narrow screens.

drops.title: Cursors, Generated
drops.description: Canvas to PNG data URL to cursor: url(…) x y — a real OS cursor with an exact hotspot, not a div chasing the pointer.
drops.concept: Custom cursors are everywhere in 2026, and almost all of them are an absolutely-positioned element trailing the real pointer — which lags, cannot leave the document and breaks over a scrollbar. This does it the other way: each shape is drawn to an offscreen canvas, exported with toDataURL and handed straight to the cursor property with its hotspot coordinates, so the operating system draws it. Six zones each carry their own bitmap with a keyword fallback, and a forge lets you set shape, size, weight, hue and hotspot while a magnified view shows the actual pixels the OS receives.
drops.source: MDN — the CSS cursor property and its url() image syntax

interaction.mouse: Move between the six zones to swap cursors; draw on the surface to see where the hotspot really is.
interaction.click: Pick a shape, drag the hotspot sliders and watch the ink separate from the crosshair.
interaction.touch: There is no pointer to replace, so each card shows its generated bitmap inline instead.

drops.title: Your Own Text Surface
drops.description: EditContext hands you the text-input state — insertions, selection, IME composition ranges, OS bounds — and draws none of it.
drops.concept: Every rich editor on the web has been a fight with contenteditable or a textarea hidden under the thing you can actually see. EditContext splits the problem: the browser owns text input, including IME composition and the bounds the OS needs for a candidate window, and the page owns every pixel. Here three surfaces — none of them contenteditable — render their own glyphs, caret, selection and composition underline from textupdate, textformatupdate and characterboundsupdate, with caret movement and Enter handled by the page because they were never the API's job. One of the three is deliberately driven by the old hidden-textarea trick, for contrast.
drops.source: Chrome for Developers — introducing the EditContext API

interaction.mouse: Click to place the caret, drag to select; every glyph and the caret are drawn by the page.
interaction.click: Switch caret style, blink and token colours — all page decisions, not browser ones.
interaction.touch: Tapping focuses a surface and the on-screen keyboard drives it through the same events.
